mcqs.question: Why is adding a cache or message queue to the very first architecture sketch, before showing a need for it, a red flag to interviewers?
options: It suggests the candidate is pattern-matching to a memorized template rather than deriving the design from stated requirements
Caches and queues are never appropriate for interview-scale problems
Diagrams are only allowed to contain four boxes
It makes the diagram too complex to fit on one whiteboard
mcqs.explanation: Starting simple and adding infrastructure only when a requirement justifies it shows derivation, not memorization; jumping straight to a cache or queue without motivation suggests a template being replayed. There's no box-count rule, and caches/queues are often exactly right later — just not unmotivated on the first pass.

mcqs.question: Why label a diagram box "cache" instead of "Redis" when first sketching a high-level design?
options: Redis cannot be drawn as a box in standard diagramming notation
Naming by responsibility keeps the conversation on trade-offs and makes the implementation swappable, rather than committing to every property of one specific product
Interviewers penalize any mention of a specific product name
Cache and Redis mean different things architecturally and cannot be used interchangeably
mcqs.explanation: Responsibility-first labels (cache, queue, rate limiter) keep the design about what the component does, letting you introduce a specific product as a detail afterward. Interviewers don't ban product names outright — the risk is only in naming the box itself after one, which locks you into defending that product's specifics.

mcqs.question: When should a candidate default to deep-then-broad instead of broad-then-narrow when building the high-level design?
options: Always — depth is more impressive than coverage in every system design round
Whenever the estimated scale is very large
Only when the interviewer has explicitly scoped the question to one flow, like "just design the write path"
Never — broad-then-narrow is the only acceptable order
mcqs.explanation: Broad-then-narrow is the safer default because most rounds expect full-system coverage; deep-then-broad only fits when the interviewer has explicitly narrowed scope to one path. It isn't about scale size, and deep-then-broad isn't universally banned — just riskier as a default.

mcqs.question: An interviewer introduces a new constraint mid-interview that the candidate's diagram doesn't account for. What's the strongest response?
options: Explain why the original diagram already implicitly handles it
Erase the whole diagram and start over from scratch
Note the constraint but continue with the original design unchanged
Point at the specific affected box and describe the change needed there, keeping the rest of the diagram intact
mcqs.explanation: Updating just the affected part of the diagram shows you're tracking the conversation and treating the sketch as a living model — the strongest response of the four. Defending the original design or ignoring the constraint reads as inflexibility; a full restart wastes the work already shown to be correct.
